title: Public Developer API Design Review
transcript:
API Lead (Sandra Ho): We're designing the v1 public API. Key decisions today: versioning strategy, auth model, rate limiting, and error format. Let's start with versioning.
Senior Dev (Pete Morgan): I strongly prefer URL versioning — /v1/, /v2/. It's explicit, easy to test, no magic.
Dev (Laila Hassan): Header versioning is cleaner — keeps URLs stable. Accept: application/vnd.company.v2+json.
Sandra: What do our top three competitors do?
Pete: Stripe uses URL versioning. Twilio uses URL. GitHub uses header.
Laila: Stripe is the gold standard for developer experience. I'd follow them.
Sandra: URL versioning it is. Auth model?
Pete: API keys for server-to-server, OAuth 2.0 with PKCE for user-delegated access.
Dev (Omar Javed): Are we supporting both from day one or phasing?
Sandra: API keys at launch, OAuth in the first major update. Too much complexity to ship both simultaneously.
Omar: Rate limiting — what's the model?
Sandra: Token bucket, per API key. Burst of 100 requests, sustained at 30 per second. Headers to communicate remaining quota.
Pete: RateLimit-Remaining, RateLimit-Reset. Standard.
Laila: Error format — I'm proposing RFC 7807 Problem Details. It's become a de facto standard.
Sandra: Example?
Laila: JSON with type, title, status, detail, instance. Machine-readable and human-readable.
Pete: I've seen developers rely on HTTP status codes and ignore error bodies. Let's make sure the detail field is always actionable.
Omar: What about pagination? Cursor-based or offset?
Sandra: Cursor-based. It handles real-time data correctly and doesn't break on inserts.
Omar: Agreed. And we should include next_cursor and has_more in every paginated response.
Sandra: Let's set a docs-first policy — every endpoint gets OpenAPI spec before any implementation starts. Pete, can you set up the Swagger scaffold this week?
Pete: Done by Wednesday.
Sandra: Laila, can you draft the error handling guidelines doc?
Laila: I'll have a draft by end of week.
summary: The developer API v1 design meeting finalized key architectural decisions: URL-based versioning following Stripe's model, API key authentication at launch with OAuth 2.0 in the first update, token bucket rate limiting at 30 req/s sustained, RFC 7807 Problem Details error format, and cursor-based pagination. A docs-first policy was established requiring OpenAPI specs before implementation.
action_items: Pete to set up OpenAPI/Swagger scaffold for the v1 API by Wednesday
Laila to draft error handling guidelines document using RFC 7807 format by end of week
Sandra to document the rate limiting model and header conventions for developer docs
Omar to write pagination spec including cursor format and response structure
Sandra to schedule API design review with developer experience team before implementation begins
decisions: URL versioning adopted (/v1/, /v2/) following Stripe's model
API key authentication at launch, OAuth 2.0 with PKCE added in first major update
RFC 7807 Problem Details format adopted for all error responses
Cursor-based pagination selected over offset pagination

PM (Lena Park): I can support a 3. I'll also note our confidence should be higher — we have strong data on user behavior around notifications.
Kim: Okay, moving notifications center impact to 3, confidence to 90%. That gives it a RICE of 810. It moves to second on the list.
Theo: What's first?
Kim: Bulk actions — RICE of 940. High reach, high impact, low effort.
Lena: Bulk actions is a classic enterprise request. I agree with the ranking.
PM (Omar Farouk): I want to flag report scheduling — it's ranked eighth but I think effort is overestimated. You have it at 8 weeks. Engineering told me last week it would be 3 to 4 weeks.
Kim: Really? That changes the RICE significantly. Omar, can you get that estimate in writing from engineering before we finalize?
Omar: I'll have it by tomorrow morning.
Kim: Let's hold report scheduling's final rank until we have the updated estimate. For everything else, top three for Q3 are bulk actions, notifications center, and CSV export. Any objections?
Lena: CSV export is bottom of my list personally — so much engineering effort for something we could solve with a lighter solution.
Kim: What's the lighter solution?
Lena: Direct download from the data grid. Half the effort, 80% of the value.
Kim: Let's explore that. Can you write a one-pager on the lightweight alternative by Thursday?
Lena: Yes.
summary: The RICE scoring session evaluated nine features for Q3 prioritization. Bulk actions ranked first (940), notifications center was rescored upward to second (810) after impact and confidence adjustments. CSV export's ranking is under review after a lightweight alternative was proposed, and report scheduling requires an updated engineering estimate before final ranking.

Sara: Smart use of existing structure.

title: IT Infrastructure and Security Posture Review
transcript:
CISO (Rachel Moore): Quarterly security posture review. Three areas: vulnerability management, access control, and incident readiness.
VP Engineering (Ben Osei): Start with vulnerabilities — I want to understand our exposure.
Rachel: We ran a full vulnerability scan last week. 127 open vulnerabilities identified. Eight are critical, 34 high, 85 medium and low.

Ben: Unpatched Apache servers — how is that still open?
Raj: They're in the staging environment. They've been deprioritized.
Rachel: Staging environment vulnerabilities can be pivoted to production in a sophisticated attack. They're not acceptable.
Ben: Agreed. Patch this week.
Raj: Will do.
Rachel: Access control — we conducted an access audit. 47 employees have access to production technicals they no longer need based on their current role. Classic access creep.
CTO (Yuki Sato): That's a real risk. Ex-employees?
Rachel: No, all current employees. But they've changed roles or their projects have ended.
Rachel: I'm implementing a quarterly access review process. We'll use an automated report from our IAM technical.

Ben: That's too long. What's the target?
Rachel: Industry standard is 30 minutes for a customer-impacting incident. I'm drafting a template and playbook.
CTO: Have it ready by next month's review.
summary: The IT security posture review found 8 critical vulnerabilities including unpatched Apache servers in staging, 47 employees with excess production access, and a customer incident communication gap (90 minutes to first notification vs 30-minute target).
